 `./README.md`

````text
1	# SE AI Agent Index
2	
3	A dataset and retrieval tool for analyzing **Software Engineering (SE) practices** of AI agents, built using a semi-automated approach that combines LLM-assisted information extraction with qualitative analysis and manual validation.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Dataset
8	
9	### Final Index (XLSX)
10	
11	- **Location:** [`data/dataset/Index.xlsx`](data/dataset/Index.xlsx) or [`data/dataset/Index.pdf`](data/dataset/Index.pdf)
12	- Manually curated and validated final index
13	- 13 agents × 7 SE dimensions in a structured table
14	- Each cell contains information items (summarized findings with source evidence)
15	
16	### Final JSON
17	
18	- **Location:** [`data/Indexing/`](data/Indexing/) — one JSON file per agent
19	- Machine-readable format with embedded `q_id` fields for direct lookup
20	- Contains raw summaries, verbatim evidence quotes, and source citations
21	
22	---
23	
24	### How to Use the Final Index
25	
26	The Final Index is organized as a table with agent metadata followed by SE dimension columns:
27	
28	- **Rows (13):** One row per indexed agent — name, description, and repository metadata
29	- **Columns:** Agent description, metadata, then 7 SE dimensions — SE Methodology, Code Review, Testing, CI/CD, Issue Resolution, Communication, and Documentation
30	
31	13 agents indexed across 7 SE dimensions. Each dimension contains information about four sub-dimensions: **Practices**, **Tools**, **Stakeholders**, and **Others**.
32	
33	---
34	
35	### How to Use the Final JSON
36	
37	Each file in [`data/Indexing/`](data/Indexing/) follows this structure. Every summary object has a `q_id` as its first field for direct lookup by dimension and sub-dimension:
38	
39	```jsonc
40	{
41	  "Agent_Name": "...",
42	  "Description": [{ "q_id": "q_1", "Summary": "...", "evidence": [{ "quote": "...", "citation": "[1]" }] }],
43	  "Repository_Statistics": { "Stars": [...], "Contributors": [...], "Lines_of_Code": [...], "Update_Frequency": [...], "Primary_Language": [...] },
44	  "SE_Practices": {
45	    "Testing_and_Reliability":               { "Practices": [...], "Tools": [...], "Stakeholders": [...], "Others": [...] },
46	    "Integration_and_Infrastructure_CICD":   { ... },
47	    "Code_Review_Process":                   { ... },
48	    "Bug_Solving_Approaches":                { "Issues": [...], "Practices": [...], "Tools": [...], "Stakeholders": [...], "Others": [...] },
49	    "Software_Engineering_Methodology":      { ... },
50	    "Team_Communication":                    { ... },
51	    "Holistic_Documentation":                { ... }
52	  },
53	  "References": { "[1]": { "Website_Type": "...", "Link": "...", "Date_Created": "...", "Date_Pulled": "YYYY-MM-DD" } }
54	}
55	```
56	
57	---
58	
59	### Examples Used in the Paper
60	
61	| Agent Name              | Example In the Paper                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Reference                                                                                                                                                                         |
62	| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
63	| HubSpot Breeze Studio   | Adopts the [Testing Trophy](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/the-testing-trophy-and-testing-classifications) strategy, prioritizing integration tests as the best balance between confidence and maintenance cost                                                                                         | [kentcdodds.com/blog/the-testing-trophy-and-testing-classifications](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/the-testing-trophy-and-testing-classifications)                                   |
64	| IBM WatsonX Orchestrate | Uses [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) to trace agent trajectories and monitor hallucinations and token usage                                                                                                                                                                               | [community.ibm.com/.../debug-with-confidence](https://community.ibm.com/community/user/blogs/bruno-fernandes-dos-santos/2026/04/13/debug-with-confidence-the-new-debug-experience) |
65	| Browser Use             | Supports two sandboxing strategies: (1) only risky operations run in a sandbox while the agent runs on the backend, or (2) the entire agent runs in a sandbox with a proxy holding all API keys; migrated from (1) to (2) for scalability and security                                              | [browser-use.com/posts/two-ways-to-sandbox-agents](https://browser-use.com/posts/two-ways-to-sandbox-agents)                                                                       |
66	| IBM WatsonX Orchestrate | The [Agent Development Kit (ADK)](https://developer.watson-orchestrate.ibm.com/) ships with a built-in red-teaming command that simulates 15+ attack types, including prompt injection and instruction override                                                                                      | [developer.watson-orchestrate.ibm.com/evaluate/llm_vulnerability](https://developer.watson-orchestrate.ibm.com/evaluate/llm_vulnerability)                                         |
67	| HubSpot Breeze Studio   | Migrated its code-review system from [Sidekick](https://product.hubspot.com/blog/automated-code-review-the-6-month-evolution) to [Aviator](https://product.hubspot.com/blog/automated-code-review-the-6-month-evolution), a Java-based agent framework; the migration reduced time-to-feedback by 90% | [product.hubspot.com/blog/automated-code-review-the-6-month-evolution](https://product.hubspot.com/blog/automated-code-review-the-6-month-evolution)                               |
68	| Browser Use             | Uses [Gemini 2.5 Flash](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini/) as an [LLM-as-judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685) to evaluate whether web agents successfully completed browsing tasks, achieving 87% alignment with human labels                                                                | [browser-use.com/posts/our-browser-agent-evaluation-system](https://browser-use.com/posts/our-browser-agent-evaluation-system)                                                     |

83	## Retrieval Tool
84	
85	A retrieval tool for querying the SE index by agent and `q_id`. Clone the repository and run the shell script to look up any agent's practices, tools, stakeholders, or evidence quotes directly from the JSON files.
86	
87	```bash
88	git clone https://github.com/musta55/se-ai-agent-index.git
89	cd se-ai-agent-index
90	./se_index.sh query "Agent Name" "q-5"
91	```
92	
93	### Tool Structure
94	
95	```
96	se-ai-agent-index/
97	├── se_index.sh                  Main CLI (run from project root)
98	├── index_prompt.md              Research methodology & JSON schema
99	├── data/
100	│   ├── dataset/                 Master dataset (Index.xlsx, Index.pdf)
101	│   ├── Indexing/                Raw SE index JSON files (one per agent)
102	│   │   ├── <Agent_Name>_se_index.json   SE index output per agent
103	│   │   └── pull_sources.py              Downloads reference URLs into data/web_sources/
104	│   └── web_sources/             Cached reference files — auto-populated after index creation
105	│       └── <Agent_Name>/        One folder per agent ([N].html / [N].md / [N].yml)
106	└── tool/
107	    ├── se_index_core.py         Shared q-id logic
108	    ├── agents_config.json       Agent registry (id, name, status, reviewed)
109	    ├── build_query_index.py     Builds query_index.json from curated Excel
110	    ├── query_index.json         Generated: (agent, q-id) → summary + evidence
111	    └── query_runner.py          Query backend (called by se_index.sh)
112	```
113	
114	### Setup
115	
116	No API key is required to query the existing index:
117	
118	```bash
119	python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
120	pip install openpyxl
121	```
122	
123	### Usage
124	
125	```bash
126	# Query the index by agent and q-id
127	./se_index.sh query "Agent Name" "q-5"
128	./se_index.sh query "Browser Use" "q-5"
129	
130	# List all available q-ids for an agent
131	./se_index.sh list-queries "Agent Name"
132	./se_index.sh list-queries "Browser Use"
133	
134	# List all indexed agents
135	./se_index.sh agents
136	# → HubSpot Breeze Studio, IBM WatsonX Orchestrate, Anthropic Claude Code, ...
137	
138	# Rebuild query_index.json from the curated Excel
139	python3 tool/build_query_index.py
140	```
141	
142	---
143	
144	## Dataset Extension
145	
146	To index a new agent and extend the dataset, you need an Anthropic API key and the Claude Code CLI.
147	
148	**Install dependencies:**
149	
150	```bash
151	cp .env.example .env        # add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
152	python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
153	pip install anthropic openpyxl
154	# install Claude Code CLI: https://claude.ai/download
155	```
156	
157	**Workflow:**
158	
159	1. **Index** — `./se_index.sh index "New Agent"` researches the agent and writes `data/Indexing/new_agent_se_index.json` with embedded q-ids, then automatically downloads all reference sources to `data/web_sources/New_Agent/`.
160	2. **Curate** — Manually transfer data into `data/dataset/Index.xlsx`, verifying each claim against downloaded sources in `data/web_sources/`.
161	3. **Build index** — `python3 tool/build_query_index.py` rebuilds `tool/query_index.json`.
162	4. **Verify** — `./se_index.sh query "New Agent" "q-1"`.
163	
164	```bash
165	# Index a new agent (research + auto-download sources, 3–10 min)
166	./se_index.sh index "Agent Name"
167	
168	# Re-download reference sources
169	./se_index.sh sources "Agent Name"
170	./se_index.sh sources --all
171	```

```text
1	SE AI Agent Index: A Dataset of Software
2	Engineering Practices for Agentic AI Systems
3	Mustahid Hasan
4	William & Mary, USA
5	mhasan02@wm.edu
6	Antu Saha
7	William & Mary, USA
8	asaha02@wm.edu
9	Oscar Chaparro
10	William & Mary, USA
11	oscarch@wm.edu
12	Abstract—Agentic AI systems have rapidly expanded across
13	domains through autonomous reasoning, tool use, and task
14	execution capabilities. As organizations increasingly deploy these
15	systems in production, the software engineering (SE) practices
16	behind their development and maintenance become valuable
17	knowledge for industry practitioners, researchers, and educators.
18	However, this knowledge remains scattered across engineering
19	blogs, technical documentation, and repositories, making it diffi-
20	cult to understand how teams engineer agentic systems in practice.
21	To address this gap, we present theSE AI Agent Index, a structured
22	dataset documenting the publicly reported software engineering
23	practices of 14 industrial AI agents, a stratified sample of the
24	30 agents in the 2025 AI Agent Index, across seven dimensions,
25	including software methodologies, testing, code review, CI/CD,
26	issue resolution, communication, and documentation. The dataset
27	contains 624 information items extracted from publicly available
28	sources and organized into practices, tools, stakeholders, and other
29	relevant information, each traceable to verbatim quotations from
30	its sources. We constructed the dataset using a semi-automated
31	methodology that combines LLM-assisted information extraction,
32	manual synthesis and refinement, and validation by two authors.
33	To demonstrate its utility, we present usage scenarios showing how
34	the dataset can support industry practitioners and researchers in
35	understanding and studying the engineering of modern AI agents.
36	I. INTRODUCTION
37	Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents—autonomous programs
38	that plan multi-step workflows, invoke tools, and act on behalf
39	of users with minimal human involvement—have rapidly moved
40	from research prototypes to production deployments [ 1], [2],
41	[3]. These agents have expanded across domains from scientific
42	research and healthcare to finance, enterprise automation, and
43	notably software engineering (SE), fundamentally altering
44	how complex work is structured by automating development
45	workflows such as code generation and program repair [ 1], [4].
46	Given the autonomy of agentic systems and the non-
47	deterministic nature of Large Language Models (LLMs),
48	building and maintaining these systems likely differs from build-
49	ing traditional software [ 5], [6]. Agentic systems must operate
50	under uncertain model behavior, coordinate tool interactions,
51	and manage long-running workflows. These characteristics in-
52	troduce new SE challenges in testing, observability, deployment,
53	debugging, and maintenance [ 5], which require engineering
54	teams to continuously adapt their development and operational
55	practices. However, despite the rapid deployment of AI agents,
56	the SE practices of the organizations that build and maintain
57	these systems remain underexplored by the research community.
58	Existing efforts to document AI systems and agents,
59	including model cards [7] and system cards [8], primarily focus
60	on documenting model characteristics, intended uses, risks,
61	and governance mechanisms. Similarly, the AI Agent Index [ 9]
62	documents agents by systematically collecting evidence about
63	their technical capabilities (e.g., tool use, coding assistance,
64	web interaction, and autonomy), safety measures, deployment
65	characteristics, and governance structures. However, these
66	efforts do not document the software engineering practices
67	of the teams who build and maintain these systems, including
68	the testing methodologies, CI/CD pipelines, code review
69	processes, issue-resolution workflows, and documentation
70	practices followed throughout development and operation.
71	To fill this gap, we introduce theSE AI Agent Index: the
72	first structured dataset that documents the publicly reported
73	software engineering practices used to develop, maintain,
74	and evolve deployed AI agents. The dataset contains 624
75	information items collected from 14 industrial AI agents, a
76	stratified sample by agent categories of the 30 agents in the
77	2025 AI Agent Index [ 9], spanning chat-based agents with tool
78	access, browser-based agents, and enterprise workflow agent
79	platforms. These information items capture practices, tools,
80	stakeholders, and other relevant information across seven SE
81	dimensions: methodologies, code review, testing, CI/CD, issue
82	resolution, communication, and documentation. To construct
83	the dataset, we adopted a semi-automated methodology
84	that combines LLM-assisted information extraction from
85	publicly available sources with manual qualitative analysis and
86	validation. To ensure the reliability of the extracted information,
87	two authors validated every information item against its original
88	sources. The resulting dataset provides evidence-backed and
89	traceable documentation of how AI-agent development teams
90	report that they engineer, test, deploy, and maintain AI agents.
91	Beyond serving as a curated repository of SE practices, the
92	SE AI Agent Indexprovides a foundation for research, education,
93	and practice in AI-agent engineering. It enables comparative
94	studies of deployed agents, supports evidence-based teaching
95	through real-world case studies, and offers practitioners
96	insights into current engineering practices. Together, these
97	applications help advance the understanding of how AI agents
98	are developed, deployed, and maintained in practice.
99	II. THESE AI AGENTINDEX
100	TheSE AI Agent Indexis a collection ofpractices,tools,
101	stakeholders, andotherinformation about the development,
102	
103	=====PAGE=====
104	maintenance, and evolution of 14 industrial AI agents. The
105	data is structured and indexed in sevenSE dimensionsand
106	is stored as a spreadsheet table, with intermediate files and
107	supporting tooling to retrieve and access theinformation items
108	stored in the index. These items were extracted from publicly
109	available sources, including agents’ developer blogs, project
110	repositories, and official documentation.
111	A. AI Agents
112	The 14 AI agents of our dataset are a stratified sample of the
113	30 agents documented in the 2025 AI Agent Index [ 9], which
114	contains information about the origins, design, capabilities,
115	ecosystem, and safety features of state-of-the-art AI agents,
116	based on publicly available information and developer feedback.
117	To ensure diversity of agents and domains, we sampled the
118	agents across the three categories of the index, approximately
119	proportionally to their size: 5 of 12 chat-based agents with
120	tool access (Anthropic Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Google
121	Gemini CLI, Google Gemini, Kimi OK Computer); 3 of 5
122	browser-based agents (Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, Alibaba
123	Mobile Agent); and 6 of 13 enterprise workflow agent platforms
124	(Google Gemini Enterprise, Glean Agents, IBM watsonx
125	Orchestrate, HubSpot Breeze Studio, Browser Use, n8n).
126	These agents cover domains such as software development,
127	browser automation, and enterprise business processes.
128	B. Information Items and Dimensions
129	Our dataset comprises specific facts (i.e.,information items)
130	about an agent’s development and maintenance, across four
131	categories:practices,tools,stakeholders, andotherrelevant
132	information. These facts, extracted from publicly available
133	sources and synthesized via qualitative analysis (described
134	in Section III), are organized into seven dimensions. Five
135	dimensions follow the phases of the traditional software
136	development life cycle (planning, implementation and review,
137	testing, deployment, and maintenance), and two dimensions
138	capture concerns that span all phases: communication, as part
139	of professional practice [10], and documentation:
140	• SE Methodologies: facts about overall software develop-
141	ment/maintenance workflows and methodologies, including
142	sprint organization, team size, and planning practices.
143	• Code Review: facts about how code review is performed,
144	including pull request policies, approval requirements, and
145	code/pull request quality checks.
146	• Testing: facts about how the agents are verified and
147	validated, including test frameworks, coverage targets, and
148	testing/evaluation strategies.
149	• CI/CD: facts about continuous integration/deployment
150	(CI/CD) pipelines, including deployment processes, release
151	practices, and rollback procedures.
152	• Issue Resolution: facts about the issue resolution process,
153	including issue triage workflows, debugging approaches,
154	and recurring engineering problems.
155	• Communication and onboarding: facts about agent de-
156	velopers’ internal communication channels and contributor
157	onboarding processes.
158	• Documentation: facts about project documentation culture,
159	knowledge-sharing blogs, and other related topics.
160	The index also contains contextual information about each
161	agent, such as a general description of the agent and its features,
162	whether it is open- or closed-source, programming languages,
163	and meta-data such as # of contributors, releases, and stars.
164	Each information item in the index (e.g., a specific testing
165	practice or tool used by an agent’s development team) is
166	traceable to supporting evidence. For each agent, extracted
167	quotations (verbatim phrases from the sources) and source
168	metadata are stored in a structured JSON file alongside the
169	final spreadsheet index. Each item is uniquely identified and
170	linked to its quotations and sources, enabling users to retrieve
171	the original supporting evidence. This design facilitates auditing,
172	verification, and future updates of the dataset while preserving
173	transparency throughout the indexing process (see Section III).
174	C. Index Implementation and Tooling
175	The information items extracted and validated from the
176	sources are stored in spreadsheet table (see index.xlsx
177	or index.pdf in our dataset repository [ 11]), where each
178	row corresponds to an agent, each column corresponds to
179	an information category for a given dimension (e.g., CI/CD
180	practices or code review tools), and each cell includes a list
181	of textual statements corresponding to the information items
182	(each uniquely identified). Each of the seven dimensions spans
183	four columns:practices,tools,stakeholders, andothers.
184	The information items were synthesized and validated
185	using the methodology described in Section III. The
186	items are traceable to quotations extracted from the
187	sources. These quotations and corresponding sources (their
188	URLs) are stored in a JSON file for each agent named
189	[agent_name]_se_index.json and are also organized
190	into the seven dimensions and four information categories (prac-
191	tices, tools,etc.). Each source is uniquely identified with a num-
192	ber and has two associated dates: thecreation date(extracted
193	from the source when available), and theretrieved date(indi-
194	cates when we processed the source to extract the quotations).
195	To easily retrieve the quotations and information sources for
196	a given information item (identified by “q-id”,e.g., “q-2”), we
197	developed a script that can be executed as: ./se_index.sh
198	query <agent_name> <q-id>.
199	D. Dataset Statistics
200	As of November 6, 2026, the dataset spans 14 agents and
201	624 information items across seven dimensions and information
202	types (31 to 73 per agent, 44.6 on average). The index cites 415
203	distinct sources (8 to 58 per agent, 29.6 on average), retrieved
204	between April and November 2026. The sources span GitHub
205	repositories, issues, and repository records (48.0%); official
206	documentation and engineering blogs of the agents’ organi-
207	zations (39.3%); and other sources (12.8%) such as technical
208	papers, practitioner interviews and podcasts, and news articles.
209	III. DATASETCONSTRUCTIONMETHODOLOGY
210	Our goal was to identify and systematically document
211	information about the engineering and maintenance of the

285	Fig. 1: Methodology for extracting, synthesizing, and validating the information items in theSE AI Agent Index.
286	14 AI agents in the index. To this end, we adopted a semi-
287	automated approach that combines LLM-assisted information
288	extraction with qualitative analysis and manual validation.
289	The overall process, shown in Figure 1, consisted of three
290	phases: (1) generation of an initial index from publicly available
291	sources, (2) synthesis and refinement of the extracted informa-
292	tion, and (3) two-author validation of the resulting dataset.
293	A. Phase 1: LLM-Assisted Initial Indexing
294	For indexing the practices of the AI agent, we developed
295	a structured prompt and executed it using CLAUDESONNET-
296	4.6 Claude Code CLI to generate an initial JSON index. The
297	JSON schema mirrored the final dataset structure; the seven
298	SE dimensions, and the four information categories described
299	in Section II-B.
300	The prompt (see index_prompt.md in [11]) specified the
301	indexing objective, agent name, output schema, definitions of
302	the SE dimensions, and instructions for identifying relevant evi-
303	dence from publicly available sources. We instructed the model
304	to search and collect information from diverse source types,
305	including project repositories, official documentation, engineer-
306	ing blogs, issue trackers, technical papers, and other publicly
307	available materials. For each source, the model was asked to ex-
308	tract SE-related information, generate summaries, and provide
309	supporting verbatim quotations linked to the original source.
310	The prompt was developed iteratively by the first and third
311	authors. We initially defined the dimensions, then progressively
312	refined the prompt by introducing detailed categories, clarifying
313	the distinction between product features and development prac-
314	tices, and adding constraints to reduce irrelevant information
315	extraction. Throughout this process, we reviewed the generated
316	outputs and refined the prompt accordingly with three of the
317	14 agents: Claude Code, Browser Use, and Glean Agents.
318	B. Phase 2: Index Synthesis and Refinement
319	The initial JSON index for each agent was manually reviewed
320	by the first author, who examined every generated summary,
321	supporting quotation, and source reference to verify correctness
322	and relevance. During this process, the author synthesized val-
323	idated information items (i.e., facts) into the final spreadsheet-
324	based index. Each validated summary was converted into one
325	or more information items and assigned to the appropriate
326	dimension and information category (practices, tools,etc.).
327	Information unrelated to SE practices, such as product features,
328	marketing content or end-user functionality, was excluded.
329	The author also verified that quotations were verbatim
330	excerpts from the cited sources, checked whether quotations
331	adequately supported the generated summaries, removed in-
332	accessible or invalid sources, corrected extraction errors, and
333	identified omitted information when present in the cited source.
334	For dimensions or categories where the model reported that
335	no relevant information was found, the author performed
336	additional manual web searches to confirm the absence of
337	publicly available evidence or to add and process new sources.
338	C. Phase 3: Index Validation
339	To ensure the index quality, the second author independently
340	validated it by performing three tasks: (1) checking the
341	correctness of each information item, (2) analyzing the LLM
342	summaries excluded in Phase 2, and (3) analyzing the extracted
343	sources. For the first task, the author inspected each information
344	item against its supporting quotations and sources. The author
345	checked whether the synthesized information is correct and
346	whether the quotations and sources provide sufficient evidence,
347	and looked for missing references and broken traceability
348	links. The author agreed with 592 of the 624 items (94.9%).
349	The second author performed the other two tasks on stratified
350	random samples (95% confidence level, 10% margin of error).
351	For the second task, the author reviewed the 57 sampled LLM
352	summaries (stratified by agent, dimension, and information cat-
353	egory) in the JSON files that the first author excluded in Phase
354	2. The author agreed with 44 exclusions (77.2%), and noted
355	suggestions to enhance the index for the remaining cases. For
356	the third task, the author checked that the source is accessible,
357	that its quotations are verbatim and support the citing items, and
358	whether it contains information missing from both the JSON
359	files and the index. For 69 out of 78 sources (88.5%), the author
360	agreed with the information items extracted from them, and then
361	later the first and second authors engaged in a discussion session
362	to reach a consensus on all disagreements and updated the final
363	index accordingly. The most common reason for the disagree-
364	ments was misinterpretation of the JSON summary or source.
365	IV. INDEXUSAGESCENARIOS ANDEXAMPLES
366	TheSE AI Agent Indexcan be used bydeveloperswho
367	build, deploy, and maintain AI agents;researcherswho need
368	to understand AI agent engineering in practice; andeducators
369	who need to teach how industrial AI agents are engineered and
370	operated. This section presents representative examples from
371	the index; source citations are omitted due to space constraints.
372	
373	=====PAGE=====
374	The README file in the dataset repository [ 11] provides the
375	same examples with their corresponding references.
376	A. AI Agent Developers
377	AI agent developers can use our index to:
378	1) Assess internal engineering practices against high-
379	maturity scenarios.For example, OpenAI’s Codex team
380	reviews every pull request with its own code-review model
381	while still requiring human review for critical code such
382	as the core agent. Six out of 14 agents from our index
383	also incorporate this practice. Teams can compare their own
384	validation and review practices against such cases.
385	2) Identify tools for addressing AI-specific engineering
386	challenges.Unlike traditional software, AI agents bring new
387	challenges such as non-deterministic responses and growing
388	token costs. To track the agents, teams use observability tools.
389	Our index shows which tool each team uses and what it
390	tracks. For example, Browser Use stores every token, prompt,
391	and cost of its evaluation runs in Laminar; HubSpot uses
392	dashboards that track token usage, and failure counts for each
393	tool; and IBM’s watsonx Orchestrate uses OpenTelemetry
394	traces to inspect each step of an agent run. Developers can
395	compare these tools and find cross-agent patterns in how they
396	are used. For instance, 6 out of 14 agents use observability
397	tools, but different one, which shows that agent teams do not
398	yet share a common observability tool.
399	3) Strengthen agent security against adversarial attacks.
400	AI agents are open to attacks such as prompt injection, and
401	browser agents are especially at risk because one hidden
402	instruction on a web page can act with the user’s rights. For
403	example, IBM’s watsonx Orchestrate Agent Development
404	Kit (ADK) ships with a built-in red-teaming command
405	that simulates more than 15 attack types, including prompt
406	injection and instruction override. Since a single successful
407	attack can misuse the user’s rights, teams can use our index
408	to learn which attacks to test for and which defenses to adopt.
409	B. Researchers
410	Researchers can use our index to:
411	Perform cross-case studies of how organizations engineer
412	and maintain agents.Researchers can compare practices
413	across agent types (e.g., browser-based, chat-based, and enter-
414	prise) and the seven dimensions in Section II-B to see whether
415	a practice is specific to one company or part of a broader trend.
416	One such trend is that agents are being used heavily to build
417	agents. For instance, more than 90% of the Codex app’s code
418	is written by Codex. AI also reviews code in 6 out of 14 agents,
419	and teams such as Browser Use and HubSpot use an LLM as a
420	judge to evaluate outputs. As a result, implementation becomes
421	less of a concern, but ensuring maintainability and validating
422	the implementation are a major developer concern. Researchers
423	can use the index to study how this shift changes SE practices.
424	C. Educators
425	Educators can use our index to:
426	1) Present case studies showing how industrial AI agents
427	are built, tested, deployed, reviewed, documented, and
428	operated at scale.With our index, educators can teach
429	students that real-world agentic systems require disciplined
430	engineering beyond prompt engineering. For instance, Glean
431	illustrates testing and code review: agents are evaluated against
432	curated datasets of real-world examples graded on binary sub-
433	metrics (completeness, tone, groundedness), while dedicated
434	pull request review agents scan code changes, flag risk areas,
435	and produce prioritized checklists to keep review quality con-
436	sistent at scale. These cases help students connect abstract SE
437	concepts to the engineering practices of deployed AI systems.
438	V. LIMITATIONS ANDTHREATS TOVALIDITY
439	Some practices are documented only at the organization level;
440	we attributed them to an agent only when no contradictory
441	evidence existed, although individual teams may deviate from
442	them. LLM-assisted extraction and human interpretation may
443	introduce errors, so we traced each item to a source quotation
444	and validated the items through independent manual reviews.
445	Our 14 agents span the chat, browser, and enterprise categories,
446	but they are prominent and well documented, so the findings
447	may not generalize to smaller or less transparent teams. Finally,
448	the index reflects evidence available up to November 06, 2026,
449	and agent practices change quickly. To support future updates,
450	we release our prompts and tools together with the source
451	references, quotations, and retrieval dates.
452	VI. RELATEDWORK
453	Prior work has examined agentic systems from several
454	complementary perspectives. The AI Agent Index [ 9]
455	documents the capabilities, deployment characteristics,
456	and safety mechanisms of deployed AI agents. Wang
457	et al.[ 12] analyzed ten widely used agent-development
458	frameworks, identifying common engineering challenges and
459	framework trade-offs. Alenezi [ 13] discussed how software
460	engineering processes may need to evolve for agentic systems.
461	More broadly, AI governance research has emphasized the
462	importance of systematic documentation and transparency [ 14].
463	Despite these contributions, no prior work systematically
464	documents how practitioners engineer and maintain deployed
465	AI agents across software engineering dimensions. We address
466	this gap by introducing the first dataset of software engineering
467	practices used in the development and maintenance of deployed
468	AI agents, enabling cross-agent analyses of agent engineering
469	in practice.
470	VII. CONCLUSION
471	We introduced theSE AI Agent Index, the first structured
472	dataset documenting the software engineering practices used
473	to develop and maintain deployed AI agents. By preserving
474	traceability to supporting evidence, the index provides a
475	transparent and reproducible foundation for studying how
476	AI agents are engineered in practice. We envision the
477	dataset supporting future empirical research and industrial
478	benchmarking as AI-agent engineering continues to evolve.
479

"""
build_query_index.py

Reads the Legacy Excel as the source of truth for cell text, remaps the old
sequential [q-N] tags to the JSON-embedded q-ids, writes the result to the
current output Excel (with corrected column layout), and also regenerates
query_index.json.

Old-sequential q-ids were assigned by iterating ORDERED_COLS in counter order.
JSON-embedded q-ids (q_60, q_61, …) are the canonical ids going forward.

Run from the SE Indexing Tool directory:
    python3 build_query_index.py
"""

import json
import os
import re

import openpyxl

from se_index_core import (
    AGENT_JSON_MAP,
    COLUMN_MAP,
    ORDERED_COLS,
    build_agent_index,
    is_real_summary,
    load_json,
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Paths
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
BASE_DIR   = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
ROOT_DIR   = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "..")
PAPER_DIR  = os.path.join(ROOT_DIR, "SE Indexing for AI Agents")
EXCEL_LEGACY = os.path.join(ROOT_DIR, "SE AI Agent Index Legacy 2.xlsx")
EXCEL_OUTPUT = os.path.join(PAPER_DIR, "Analysis of SE AI Agent Index.xlsx")
QUERY_INDEX_PATH = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "query_index.json")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Legacy column → output column mapping.
# The output Excel uses the legacy as its structural template, so the column
# positions are identical.  Map every data column 1-34 straight through.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
LEGACY_TO_CURRENT_COL = {col: col for col in range(1, 35)}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Build old-sequential q-id index (what build_agent_index used to produce)
# This lets us map [q-N] tags in the legacy Excel to (col, array_index).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def build_old_sequential_index(data):
    """Return {old_q_id: (col, array_index)} using the pre-JSON counter scheme."""
    counter = [1]
    old_qid_to_pos = {}
    for col in ORDERED_COLS:
        _, accessor = COLUMN_MAP[col]
        items = accessor(data)
        for i, item in enumerate(items):
            if not isinstance(item, dict):
                continue
            summary = item.get("Summary", "").strip()
            if not is_real_summary(summary):
                continue
            old_qid_to_pos[f"q-{counter[0]}"] = (col, i)
            counter[0] += 1
    return old_qid_to_pos


def build_qid_mapping(data):
    """
    Return {old_q_id: new_q_id} for one agent.

    old_q_id: sequential id assigned by the legacy counter scheme
    new_q_id: JSON-embedded q_id (q_60 → q-60), or fallback counter
    """
    old_qid_to_pos = build_old_sequential_index(data)

    # new q-ids keyed by (col, array_index)
    new_col_item_qids = {}   # col → {array_index → new_q_id}
    used = set()
    fallback = [1]

    def _next_fallback():
        while f"q-{fallback[0]}" in used:
            fallback[0] += 1
        qid = f"q-{fallback[0]}"
        fallback[0] += 1
        return qid

    for col in ORDERED_COLS:
        _, accessor = COLUMN_MAP[col]
        items = accessor(data)
        new_col_item_qids[col] = {}
        for i, item in enumerate(items):
            if not isinstance(item, dict):
                continue
            summary = item.get("Summary", "").strip()
            if not is_real_summary(summary):
                continue
            raw = item.get("q_id", "").strip()
            new_q_id = raw.replace("_", "-") if raw else _next_fallback()
            used.add(new_q_id)
            new_col_item_qids[col][i] = new_q_id

    mapping = {}
    for old_q_id, (col, idx) in old_qid_to_pos.items():
        new_q_id = new_col_item_qids.get(col, {}).get(idx)
        if new_q_id:
            mapping[old_q_id] = new_q_id

    return mapping


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Replace [q-N] tags inside a cell string using the mapping
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def replace_qids(text, mapping):
    """Replace every [q-N] occurrence with [new_q_id] using mapping."""
    if not text:
        return text

    def replacer(m):
        old = f"q-{m.group(1)}"
        new = mapping.get(old)
        return f"[{new}]" if new else m.group(0)

    return re.sub(r'\[q-(\d+)\]', replacer, text)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main():
    if not os.path.exists(EXCEL_LEGACY):
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"Legacy Excel not found: {EXCEL_LEGACY}\n"
            "This file is the source of truth for manually curated cell text."
        )

    wb_legacy = openpyxl.load_workbook(EXCEL_LEGACY)
    ws_legacy = wb_legacy.active

    # Use the backup as the structural template for the output workbook
    # (headers, formatting, etc.) then overwrite data rows.
    backup_path = os.path.join(ROOT_DIR, "Analysis of SE AI Agent Index.backup.xlsx")
    if os.path.exists(backup_path):
        wb_out = openpyxl.load_workbook(backup_path)
    else:
        wb_out = openpyxl.load_workbook(EXCEL_LEGACY)
    ws_out = wb_out.active

    query_index = {}

    # Iterate legacy rows (data starts at row 3)
    for row in range(3, ws_legacy.max_row + 1):
        agent_cell = ws_legacy.cell(row=row, column=1).value
        if not agent_cell:
            continue

        agent_name = str(agent_cell).strip()
        agent_key  = agent_name.lower()

        json_file = AGENT_JSON_MAP.get(agent_key)
        if not json_file:
            print(f"  [WARN] No JSON mapping for: {agent_name!r}")
            continue

        print(f"\nProcessing: {agent_name}")
        data = load_json(json_file)

        # Build query index entries (new JSON-based q-ids) for query_index.json
        agent_entries, _ = build_agent_index(data)
        query_index[agent_name] = agent_entries

        # Build old→new q-id mapping for this agent
        mapping = build_qid_mapping(data)
        print(f"  q-id mapping: {len(mapping)} entries")

        # Copy legacy cell text (with q-ids updated) into output workbook
        for legacy_col, current_col in LEGACY_TO_CURRENT_COL.items():
            legacy_val = ws_legacy.cell(row=row, column=legacy_col).value
            if legacy_val is None:
                ws_out.cell(row=row, column=current_col).value = None
                continue

            updated = replace_qids(str(legacy_val), mapping)
            ws_out.cell(row=row, column=current_col).value = updated

        # Col 32 (Bug Solving > Issues) has no legacy counterpart — leave empty.

    wb_out.save(EXCEL_OUTPUT)
    print(f"\nExcel saved: {EXCEL_OUTPUT}")

    with open(QUERY_INDEX_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(query_index, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    print(f"Query index saved: {QUERY_INDEX_PATH}")

    total = sum(len(v) for v in query_index.values())
    print(f"\nDone: {len(query_index)} agents, {total} query entries total.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

se_index_core.py

Shared q-id assignment logic used by query_runner.py and build_query_index.py.

IMPORTANT: New columns must be appended at the END of COLUMN_MAP only.
           Re-ordering or inserting into the middle will break existing q-id numbers.
"""

import json
import os

BASE_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
INDEXING_DIR = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "..", "data", "Indexing")

}

CATEGORY_ALIASES = {
    "testing":      ["Testing_and_Evaluation",        "Testing_and_Reliability"],
    "cicd":         ["CICD_and_Deployment",            "Integration_and_Infrastructure_CICD"],
    "code_review":  ["Code_Review",                    "Code_Review_Process"],
    "bug_solving":  ["Bug_Solving_and_Issue_Tracking", "Bug_Solving_Approaches"],
    "methodology":  ["SE_Methodology",                 "Software_Engineering_Methodology"],
    "team_comm":    ["Team_Communication"],
    "docs":         ["Holistic_Documentation"],
    "llm":          ["LLM_Integration_and_Prompt_Management"],
}


def _normalize_desc_item(item):
    """Normalize a Description item to always have a 'Summary' key.

    Some JSON files store Description as {"value": "...", "evidence": [...]}
    instead of {"Summary": "...", "evidence": [...]}. This normalizes both.
    """
    if not isinstance(item, dict):
        return item
    if "Summary" not in item and "value" in item:
        return {
            "Summary": item.get("value", ""),
            "evidence": item.get("evidence", []),
            "q_id": item.get("q_id", ""),
        }
    return item


def _get_description(data):
    desc = data.get("Description", [])
    if isinstance(desc, list):
        return [_normalize_desc_item(i) for i in desc]
    if isinstance(desc, dict):
        return [_normalize_desc_item(desc)]
    return []


def _make_accessor(cat_key, subcategory):
    aliases = CATEGORY_ALIASES[cat_key]

    def accessor(data):
        se = data.get("SE_Practices", {})
        for alias in aliases:
            cat = se.get(alias)
            if cat and isinstance(cat, dict):
                items = cat.get(subcategory, [])
                return items if isinstance(items, list) else []
        return []

    return accessor



# Column number → (human label, accessor).
# APPEND NEW COLUMNS AT THE END ONLY — inserting anywhere above q-31 shifts existing ids.
COLUMN_MAP = {
    2:  ("Description",                   _get_description),
    3:  ("Testing > Practices",           _make_accessor("testing",     "Practices")),

"""
query_runner.py

Looks up a query ID for a given agent by reading the source JSON directly
from the Indexing/ directory — no query_index.json cache required.

For Description queries (q-1 on most agents), Repository_Statistics is
automatically included in the output since it has no q-id of its own.

Usage:
    python3 query_runner.py "Agent Name" "q-5"

Called by se_index.sh:
    ./se_index.sh query "Agent Name" "q-5"
"""

import json
import sys

from se_index_core import (
    AGENT_JSON_MAP,
    build_agent_index,
    fuzzy_match_agent,
    load_json,
)


def get_repo_stats(data):
    """Return the raw Repository_Statistics dict, or None if absent/empty."""
    rs = data.get("Repository_Statistics", data.get("Repository Statistics", {}))
    return rs if rs and isinstance(rs, dict) else None


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print("Usage: python3 query_runner.py \"Agent Name\" \"q-{id}\"", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    agent_input = sys.argv[1].strip()
    # Normalise q_60, q-60, or bare 60 → q-60
    raw_qid = sys.argv[2].strip().lower()
    import re as _re
    query_id = "q-" + _re.sub(r"^q[_-]?", "", raw_qid)

    matched_key, json_file = fuzzy_match_agent(agent_input)
    if not matched_key:
        available = ", ".join(f'"{a}"' for a in sorted(AGENT_JSON_MAP.keys()))
        print(f"Error: Agent '{agent_input}' not found.", file=sys.stderr)
        print(f"Available agents: {available}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    data = load_json(json_file)
    agent_display = data.get("Agent_Name", data.get("Agent Name", matched_key))

    query_entries, _ = build_agent_index(data)

    if query_id not in query_entries:
        available = ", ".join(
            sorted(query_entries.keys(), key=lambda x: int(x.split("-")[1]))
        )
        print(f"Error: Query ID '{query_id}' not found for agent '{agent_display}'.", file=sys.stderr)
        print(f"Available IDs: {available}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    entry = query_entries[query_id]

    result = {
        "agent": agent_display,
        "query_id": query_id,
        "column": entry.get("column_label", ""),
        "summary": entry.get("summary"),
        "evidence": entry.get("evidence", []),
    }

    # Description queries include Repository_Statistics (it has no q-id of its own)
    if entry.get("column_label") == "Description":
        rs = get_repo_stats(data)
        if rs:
            result["repository_statistics"] = rs

ORDERED_COLS = sorted(COLUMN_MAP.keys())


def normalize_references(raw):
    if isinstance(raw, dict):
        return raw
    if isinstance(raw, list):
        result = {}
        for item in raw:
            if isinstance(item, dict) and "id" in item:
                result[item["id"]] = item
        return result
    return {}


def resolve_evidence(evidence_list, references):
    resolved = []
    for ev in evidence_list:
        if not isinstance(ev, dict):
            continue
        cite_str = ev.get("citation", "")
        ref_obj = references.get(cite_str, cite_str)
        resolved.append({
            "quote": ev.get("quote", "").strip(),
            "citation": ref_obj,
        })
    return resolved


def is_real_summary(summary):
    if not summary or not summary.strip():
        return False
    return not summary.strip().lower().startswith("not available")


def build_agent_index(data):
    """
    Build q-id index from JSON items.  Q-ids are taken directly from the
    'q_id' field embedded in each JSON item (e.g. "q_60" → "q-60"), so the
    spreadsheet and JSON share the same identifiers.  Items that lack a q_id
    field (e.g. old-format Description objects) fall back to a counter that
    avoids collisions with existing ids.

    Returns:
      query_entries : dict  q-id → {column_label, array_index, summary, evidence}
      col_item_qids : dict  col_num → {array_index → q-id}
    """
    references = normalize_references(data.get("References", {}))
    fallback_counter = [1]
    query_entries = {}
    col_item_qids = {}

    def _next_fallback():
        while f"q-{fallback_counter[0]}" in query_entries:
            fallback_counter[0] += 1
        qid = f"q-{fallback_counter[0]}"
        fallback_counter[0] += 1
        return qid

    for col in ORDERED_COLS:
        label, accessor = COLUMN_MAP[col]
        items = accessor(data)
        col_item_qids[col] = {}

        for i, item in enumerate(items):
            if not isinstance(item, dict):
                continue
            summary = item.get("Summary", "").strip()
            evidence = resolve_evidence(item.get("evidence", []), references)

            if not is_real_summary(summary):
                continue

            # Use the q_id embedded in the JSON (q_60 → q-60); fall back to counter.
            raw = item.get("q_id", "").strip()
            if raw:
                q_id = raw.replace("_", "-")
            else:
                q_id = _next_fallback()

            query_entries[q_id] = {
                "column_label": label,
                "array_index": i,
                "summary": summary,
                "evidence": evidence,
            }
            col_item_qids[col][i] = q_id

    return query_entries, col_item_qids


def load_json(filename):
    with open(os.path.join(INDEXING_DIR, filename), "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return json.load(f)


def fuzzy_match_agent(agent_name):
    """Case-insensitive exact match, then prefix match. Returns (key, filename) or (None, None)."""
    lower = agent_name.lower()
    for key in AGENT_JSON_MAP:
        if key == lower:
            return key, AGENT_JSON_MAP[key]
    for key in AGENT_JSON_MAP:
        if key.startswith(lower) or lower.startswith(key):
            return key, AGENT_JSON_MAP[key]
    return None, None

    sys.exit(1)
print(f"Agent: {matched}\n")

    preview = (entry['summary'] or 'Not Available')[:80].replace('\n', ' ')
    print(f"  {qid:<8} [{entry['column_label']}]  {preview}...")
PYEOF
}

cmd_agents() {

PYEOF
}

cmd_index() {

  # First time setup

  # Query the index for verification:
  ./se_index.sh query        "HubSpot Breeze Studio" "q-3"
  ./se_index.sh list-queries "Anthropic Claude Code"
  ./se_index.sh agents

# Indexed Agents

14 industrial AI agents indexed across 7 SE dimensions. The agents are a stratified sample of the 30 agents in the [2025 AI Agent Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17753), drawn from its three categories roughly in proportion to their size: 5 of 12 chat-based agents with tool access, 3 of 5 browser-based agents, and 6 of 13 enterprise workflow agent platforms.

### Chat-based agents with tool access (5 of 12)

| Agent                                                            | Description                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Anthropic Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)                  | Agentic coding CLI tool by Anthropic that lives in the terminal, understands full codebases, and autonomously executes multi-step engineering tasks via natural language.                    |
| [OpenAI Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex)                  | OpenAI's coding agent that writes features, fixes bugs, reviews code, and proposes pull requests, shipped as an open-source Rust CLI, IDE extensions, a desktop app, and a cloud agent in ChatGPT. |
| [Google Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) | Open-source, terminal-based AI coding agent that brings Gemini model capabilities directly to the command line for development tasks.                                                        |
| [Google Gemini](https://gemini.google.com/)                      | Google's multimodal AI assistant powered by the Gemini model family, capable of processing text, images, audio, video, and code across Google products and services.                         |
| [Kimi OK Computer](https://kimi.ai/)                             | Chat-based AI agent by Moonshot AI that autonomously operates a cloud computing environment to complete complex multi-step tasks including web browsing, code execution, and deep research.  |

### Browser-based agents (3 of 5)

| Agent                                                         | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Opera Neon](https://www.opera.com/one)                       | Subscription-based AI agentic browser by Opera Software that combines in-browser automation (Neon Do), conversational AI (Neon Chat), and cloud-based content creation (Neon Make).                                                 |
| [Perplexity Comet](https://www.perplexity.ai/)                | Chromium-based AI browser that combines traditional web browsing with autonomous agentic task execution through a two-layer AI architecture: an assistant for reading and summarizing, and an agent for multi-step task automation. |
| [Alibaba Mobile Agent](https://github.com/X-PLUG/MobileAgent) | Open-source cross-platform mobile GUI automation agent by Tongyi Lab at Alibaba, using a vision-language model in a four-role multi-agent framework (Manager, Worker, Reflector, Notetaker) to automate tasks on real devices.      |

````markdown
# SE AI Agent Index

The **SE AI Agent Index** is a structured dataset of the publicly reported software engineering (SE) practices of **14 industrial AI agents**, a stratified sample of the 30 agents in the [2025 AI Agent Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17753). It contains **624 information items** across **seven SE dimensions**. Each item is traceable to verbatim quotations from publicly available sources.

The dataset was built with a semi-automated method. An LLM extracted the initial information, the first author synthesized and refined it by hand, and a second author validated it.

---

## Dataset

### Agents

The 14 agents were sampled across the three categories of the 2025 AI Agent Index, roughly in proportion to each category's size:

| Category                             | Sampled | Agents                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------ | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Chat-based agents with tool access   | 5 of 12 | Anthropic Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini CLI, Google Gemini, Kimi OK Computer                      |
| Browser-based agents                 | 3 of 5  | Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, Alibaba Mobile Agent                                                           |
| Enterprise workflow agent platforms  | 6 of 13 | Google Gemini Enterprise, Glean Agents, IBM watsonx Orchestrate, HubSpot Breeze Studio, Browser Use, n8n     |

See [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for links and a short description of each agent.

### Information Items and Dimensions

An **information item** is a specific fact about how an agent is developed and maintained. Each item belongs to one of four categories: **practices**, **tools**, **stakeholders**, and **others** (other relevant information). Items are organized into seven dimensions. The first five follow the phases of the software development life cycle (planning, implementation and review, testing, deployment, and maintenance). The last two, communication and documentation, cover concerns that span all phases.

| Dimension                    | What it covers                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SE Methodologies             | Overall development/maintenance workflows, including sprint organization, team size, and planning |
| Code Review                  | Pull request policies, approval requirements, and code/pull request quality checks              |
| Testing                      | Verification and validation, including test frameworks, coverage targets, and evaluation strategies |
| CI/CD                        | Continuous integration/deployment pipelines, release practices, and rollback procedures         |
| Issue Resolution             | Issue triage workflows, debugging approaches, and recurring engineering problems                |
| Communication and onboarding | Developers' internal communication channels and contributor onboarding                          |
| Documentation                | Documentation culture, knowledge-sharing blogs, and related topics                              |

The index also records contextual information about each agent: a description of the agent and its features, whether it is open- or closed-source, its programming languages, and metadata such as the number of contributors, releases, and stars.

### Statistics

As of November 6, 2026:

- **14 agents** and **624 information items** (31 to 73 per agent, 44.6 on average)
- **415 distinct sources** (8 to 58 per agent, 29.6 on average), retrieved between April and November 2026
- Source types: GitHub repositories, issues, and repository records (48.0%); official documentation and engineering blogs of the agents' organizations (39.3%); other sources such as technical papers, practitioner interviews and podcasts, and news articles (12.8%)

---

## Files

### Index (spreadsheet)

- **Location:** [`data/dataset/Index.xlsx`](data/dataset/Index.xlsx) (also [`data/dataset/Index.pdf`](data/dataset/Index.pdf))
- Each **row** is an agent. Each **column** is one information category within a dimension (e.g., CI/CD practices or code review tools). The seven dimensions each span four columns: Practices, Tools, Stakeholders, and Others.
- Each cell holds a list of textual statements, one per information item. Each statement ends with its q-id (e.g., `[q-15]`), which links it to its quotations and sources in the JSON file.

### Evidence (JSON, one file per agent)

- **Location:** [`data/Indexing/`](data/Indexing/), named `<agent_name>_se_index.json`
- Stores the summaries, the verbatim quotations that support them, and the source references, organized into the same seven dimensions and four categories
- Each summary has a `q_id` (e.g., `q_15`), the same id cited in the spreadsheet
- Each source has a number (e.g., `[4]`) and two dates: the **creation date** (taken from the source when available) and the **retrieved date** (when we processed the source)

```jsonc
{
  "Agent_Name": "...",
  "Description": [{ "q_id": "q_1", "Summary": "...", "evidence": [{ "quote": "...", "citation": "[1]" }] }],
  "Repository_Statistics": { "Stars": [...], "Contributors": [...], "Lines_of_Code": [...], "Update_Frequency": [...], "Primary_Language": [...] },
  "SE_Practices": {
    "SE_Methodology":                 { "Practices": [...], "Tools": [...], "Stakeholders": [...], "Others": [...] },
    "Code_Review":                    { ... },
    "Testing_and_Evaluation":         { ... },
    "CICD_and_Deployment":            { ... },
    "Bug_Solving_and_Issue_Tracking": { "Issues": [...], "Practices": [...], "Tools": [...], "Stakeholders": [...], "Others": [...] },
    "Team_Communication":             { ... },
    "Holistic_Documentation":         { ... }
  },
  "References": { "[1]": { "Website_Type": "...", "Link": "...", "Date_Created": "...", "Date_Pulled": "YYYY-MM-DD" } }
}
```

Each item inside a category list has the form `{ "q_id": "q_15", "Summary": "...", "evidence": [{ "quote": "...", "citation": "[4]" }] }`.

Some files use an older set of dimension key names. The retrieval tool accepts both:

| Dimension in the paper       | JSON key                         | Older JSON key                        |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| SE Methodologies             | `SE_Methodology`                 | `Software_Engineering_Methodology`    |
| Code Review                  | `Code_Review`                    | `Code_Review_Process`                 |
| Testing                      | `Testing_and_Evaluation`         | `Testing_and_Reliability`             |
| CI/CD                        | `CICD_and_Deployment`            | `Integration_and_Infrastructure_CICD` |
| Issue Resolution             | `Bug_Solving_and_Issue_Tracking` | `Bug_Solving_Approaches`              |
| Communication and onboarding | `Team_Communication`             | —                                     |
| Documentation                | `Holistic_Documentation`         | —                                     |

---

## Construction Methodology

1. **LLM-assisted initial indexing.** A structured prompt ([`index_prompt.md`](index_prompt.md)) was run with Claude Sonnet 4.6 in the Claude Code CLI, using web search, to produce an initial JSON index for each agent. The first and third authors refined the prompt on three of the 14 agents: Claude Code, Browser Use, and Glean Agents.
2. **Synthesis and refinement.** The first author reviewed every generated summary, quotation, and source, and turned the validated summaries into the information items in the spreadsheet. Non-SE content was excluded, such as product features, marketing, and end-user functionality. The author also fixed extraction errors and removed inaccessible sources. Where the model found no information, the author searched the web by hand.
3. **Index validation.** The second author independently checked:

   | Task                                                    | Sample                          | Agreement     |
   | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------- |
   | Correctness of each information item                    | all 624 items                   | 592 (94.9%)   |
   | LLM summaries excluded in Phase 2                        | 57 summaries (stratified)       | 44 (77.2%)    |
   | Sources (accessible, verbatim quotes, missing information) | 78 sources (stratified)       | 69 (88.5%)    |

   The samples were stratified random samples at a 95% confidence level with a 10% margin of error. The first and second authors then discussed every disagreement until they reached consensus and updated the index.

---

## Examples Used in the Paper

The paper omits source citations for space. These are the same examples with their references. Look up a q-id with `./se_index.sh query "<Agent>" <q-id>` to see its quotations and sources.

---

## Retrieval Tool

Each information item has a q-id. The retrieval script returns the item's summary, verbatim quotations, and sources:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/musta55/se-ai-agent-index.git
cd se-ai-agent-index
./se_index.sh query <agent_name> <q-id>
./se_index.sh query "OpenAI Codex" "q-15"
```

### Setup

No API key is needed to query the index:

```bash
python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install openpyxl
```

### Usage

```bash
# Look up an information item by agent and q-id
./se_index.sh query "Browser Use" "q-5"

# List all q-ids for an agent
./se_index.sh list-queries "Browser Use"

# List the 14 indexed agents
./se_index.sh agents

# Rebuild tool/query_index.json (used by list-queries and agents) from the JSON files
python3 tool/build_query_index.py
```

### Repository Structure

```
se-ai-agent-index/
├── se_index.sh                  Main CLI (run from project root)
├── index_prompt.md              Indexing prompt & JSON schema (Phase 1)
├── AGENTS.md                    The 14 indexed agents
├── data/
│   ├── dataset/                 Final index (Index.xlsx, Index.pdf)
│   ├── Indexing/                Evidence JSON files (one per agent)
│   │   ├── <agent_name>_se_index.json
│   │   └── pull_sources.py      Downloads reference URLs into data/web_sources/
│   └── web_sources/             Local cache of reference sources (not tracked)
└── tool/
    ├── se_index_core.py         Shared q-id logic and agent → JSON map
    ├── agents_config.json       Agent registry (id, name, status, reviewed)
    ├── build_query_index.py     Builds query_index.json from the JSON files
    ├── query_index.json         Generated: (agent, q-id) → summary + evidence
    └── query_runner.py          Query backend (called by se_index.sh)
```

---

## Extending the Dataset

The prompts and tools are released so the index can be updated as agent practices change. To index a new agent you need an Anthropic API key and the Claude Code CLI:

```bash
cp .env.example .env        # add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install anthropic openpyxl
# install Claude Code CLI: https://claude.ai/download
```

1. **Index (Phase 1):** `./se_index.sh index "New Agent"` researches the agent and writes `data/Indexing/new_agent_se_index.json` with embedded q-ids. It then downloads the reference sources to `data/web_sources/New_Agent/`.
2. **Synthesize (Phase 2):** Check each summary against the downloaded sources, then add the validated information items, with their q-ids, to `data/dataset/Index.xlsx`.
3. **Validate (Phase 3):** Have a second person independently check the items against their quotations and sources.
4. **Register:** Add the agent to `AGENT_JSON_MAP` in `tool/se_index_core.py`, run `python3 tool/build_query_index.py`, and check the result with `./se_index.sh query "New Agent" "q-1"`.

```bash
# Re-download reference sources
./se_index.sh sources "Agent Name"
./se_index.sh sources --all
```

---

## Limitations

- Some practices are documented only at the organization level. We attributed them to an agent only when no evidence contradicted them, but individual teams may deviate.
- The 14 agents are prominent and well documented, so the findings may not generalize to smaller or less transparent teams.
- The index reflects evidence available up to November 6, 2026, and agent practices change quickly.

---

## License

Research use only. Data derived from publicly available sources.

import json, sys

next_id = max((e["id"] for e in cfg), default=0) + 1
cfg.append({"id": next_id, "agent_name": name, "indexing_status": "pending", "reviewed": False})
with open(cfg_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:

```python
"""
build_query_index.py

Regenerates tool/query_index.json from the per-agent evidence JSON files in
data/Indexing/. The index maps (agent, q-id) → summary + evidence and backs the
`list-queries` and `agents` commands of se_index.sh. (`query` reads the JSON
files directly.)

The agents included, and their display names, come from AGENT_DISPLAY_NAMES in
se_index_core.py.

Run from the project root:
    python3 tool/build_query_index.py
"""

import json
import os

from se_index_core import AGENT_DISPLAY_NAMES, build_agent_index, load_json

BASE_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
QUERY_INDEX_PATH = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "query_index.json")


def main():
    query_index = {}
    for json_file, agent_name in AGENT_DISPLAY_NAMES.items():
        entries, _ = build_agent_index(load_json(json_file))
        query_index[agent_name] = entries
        print(f"  {agent_name:<26} {len(entries):>3} q-ids  ({json_file})")

    with open(QUERY_INDEX_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(query_index, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

    total = sum(len(v) for v in query_index.values())
    print(f"\nQuery index saved: {QUERY_INDEX_PATH}")
    print(f"Done: {len(query_index)} agents, {total} query entries total.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

As of 2026-11-11, Writing/SE_AI_Agent_Index.pdf comes from a different source, probably Overleaf, than the local .tex files. The two differ in several ways:
- The PDF has Section IV "Index Usage Scenarios"; the local main has Cross-Agent Analysis and comments out 7_discussion.
- Phase 3 Task 2 is 44/57 (77.2%) in the PDF and 35/57 (61.4%) in the local tex.
- The PDF has no Garousi or Lyu text.

PDFKit text extraction via swift works when poppler is missing.

Findings from the final check (reported to the user, not yet fixed):
- **Sample-T1 labels.** The local xlsx has No 37 / Partial 5 / Yes 15. All 20 Yes and Partial summaries became Agreement Index additions. That gives a strict agreement of 37/57 (64.9%). The PDF's 44 equals No plus Partial under an older labelling (35/9/13).
- **592/624.** This count includes 23 post-T1 additions that were pre-filled as Agree, 7 items added by author 2 and counted as Disagree, and 47 System Metric rows. Without the 23 additions it is 569/601 (94.7%); for author 1's items only it is 569/594 (95.8%).
- **Gemini Enterprise traceability.** Four items cite q-ids the query tool can't resolve, because their JSON summaries are "Not Available": GEMENT-TEST-PRA-04 (q-39), GEMENT-CICD-STK-01 (q-48), GEMENT-CODEREV-STK-01 (q-57) and GEMENT-SEMETH-TOO-01 (q-68).
- **Stale repo files.** Repo Index.xlsx/Index.pdf (July), README, AGENTS.md and `se_index.sh agents` still list 13 agents, including Amazon Q.

**Why:** the user treats the PDF as the paper of record, and the local tex is out of sync.
**How to apply:** when asked to check or edit the paper, ask which source built the PDF before editing the local tex. See [[validation-samples]], [[t2-review-fixes]].

The README and AGENTS.md now match the paper: 14 agents, sampled 5 chat / 3 browser / 6 enterprise, with Amazon Q removed and OpenAI Codex and n8n added. All the CLI commands also return the same 14 agents. Nothing is committed yet.

**[README.md](README.md)**, rewritten to follow the paper:
- **Overview and counts:** the opening describes the dataset as the paper does. The statistics are copied from the paper (624 items, 415 sources, as of November 6, 2026); I did not recount them.
- **Agents:** a table of the three categories with each agent's name as the paper writes it, e.g. "IBM watsonx Orchestrate", "Kimi OK Computer", "n8n".
- **Dimensions:** the seven dimensions use the paper's names and order. A small table maps them to the JSON key names, which differ between files.
- **Methodology:** the three phases, with the validation results 592/624, 44/57 and 78 sources → 69.
- **Examples:** the paper says the README gives "the same examples with their corresponding references", so this section now holds only the Section IV examples. They are grouped by Developers / Researchers / Educators, each with its source link and q-id. All 12 q-ids resolve with `./se_index.sh query`.
- **Limitations:** a new section summarising the paper's limitations.

I made two choices you may want to change:
- **Old examples removed.** The examples that aren't in the paper are gone: the Testing Trophy, Browser Use sandboxing, the Aviator migration, the 50,000-PR and Kubernetes build-time example, and Claude Code prototyping. I can restore them under an "Additional examples" heading.
- **"6 out of 14" claims left out.** The examples tables leave out the paper's two "6 out of 14 agents" claims (AI code review and observability tools), because neither has a single source to cite.

**[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md):** the 14 agents are grouped by category, with new descriptions for Codex and n8n taken from their JSON files.

**Tooling:**
- **`agents` and `list-queries`:** they read `tool/query_index.json`, which still listed the old 13 agents. Its builder, `build_query_index.py`, was broken because it needed a legacy Excel file that no longer exists. It now rebuilds the index from the JSON files, so both commands return the 14 agents.
- **Paper names:** [tool/se_index_core.py](tool/se_index_core.py) now holds the paper's agent names. Queries accept them (e.g. "IBM watsonx Orchestrate", "n8n"), and `query` prints them.
- **Registry:** Amazon Q is removed from [tool/agents_config.json](tool/agents_config.json), and Codex and n8n are marked reviewed.
- **Local skill:** the se-index skill now says 14 agents instead of 13.

**Still open:**
- **Broken q-ids:** four Google Gemini Enterprise q-ids cited in the index (q-39, q-48, q-57, q-68) still don't resolve, because their JSON summaries are "Not Available". That goes against the README's claim that every item is traceable.
- **Amazon Q sources:** `data/web_sources/Amazon_Q_Developer/` is still tracked in git, even though `.gitignore` now ignores `data/web_sources/`. Run `git rm -r --cached data/web_sources` if you want the cached sources out of the repo.
